tldr: VisionSIM is a robotics simulation platform that physically reproduces inherent measurement failure modes in real-world sensors—such as pileup, phase wrapping, and thermal history—enabling fair comparison and evaluation of diverse heterogeneous sensor suites on identical scenes.
hero_caption: Overall concept of VisionSIM. From a single high-fidelity scene rendering pass, diverse ground truths are generated and used as shared inputs to accurately emulate the raw measurement processes and modality-specific physical failure modes of SPAD, iToF, event, and thermal cameras.
overview:
Modern robotic perception increasingly relies on combining conventional RGB cameras with diverse emerging modalities, including event cameras, single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) LiDAR, indirect Time-of-Flight (iToF), and thermal cameras. However, existing robotics simulators have idealized these sensors excessively—treating LiDAR as a mere noiseless depth generator or applying thermal images as static textures. As a result, critical measurement failure modes encountered in real-world environments (such as LiDAR pileup distortion and glare, iToF phase wrapping and motion artifacts, and thermal conduction lag) never appear in simulation, creating a severe Sim-to-Real gap where perception algorithms fail upon deployment.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed VisionSIM, a unified simulation platform that completely decouples CG rendering from sensor physics emulation. By passing ideal ray radiance and thermal data obtained from a high-fidelity rendering engine through the physical measurement process of each sensor (such as Poisson photon arrivals, dead time, demodulation correlation, and numerical solutions to the heat conduction equation), sensor non-idealities and failure modes emerge naturally. Furthermore, leveraging differentiable physical models, the authors fit physical parameters to real-world measurements, successfully constructing "digital twins" of physical sensors.

Sim-to-Real validation against physical hardware demonstrates that VisionSIM accurately matches SPAD LiDAR pileup and glare, transient temperature changes in thermal cameras, and phase errors in iToF. The authors also release a large-scale multimodal dataset spanning 100 diverse indoor environments, establishing a principled, physically grounded foundation for robot perception system design and sensor selection.
contributions: Built VisionSIM, a unified platform that decouples CG rendering from sensor emulation to physically simulate conventional cameras, SPAD (dToF), iToF, event cameras, thermal cameras, and IMUs simultaneously along identical scenes and trajectories.

Accurately reproduced sensor-specific physical failure modes at the raw data level—including pileup distortion, phase wrapping, refractory drops, and thermal inertia—which were overlooked by general-purpose simulators.

Constructed digital twins of real physical sensors (e.g., SPAD LiDAR) by identifying their parameters from physical measurements using differentiable measurement models, dramatically reducing Sim-to-Real depth errors.

Released a comprehensive dataset and generation toolchain consisting of 100 indoor scenes with 24-second trajectories, featuring perfectly synchronized raw sensor measurements and dense ground-truth annotations.

sections.heading: Why Existing Simulators Fail to Replicate a Robot's "Eyes" in the Real World
sections.summary: Robots make decisions based on noisy and distorted sensor measurements rather than idealized ground truth. While conventional simulators excel at rigid-body dynamics and visual photorealism, they neglect the physical limits of sensors, causing unexpected failures during real-world deployment.
sections.details:
When a robot operates inside a simulator, it consistently receives crisp, noiseless images and perfect range data. In the real world, however, exposure time introduces severe motion blur in cameras, single-photon LiDAR hallucinates phantom obstacles in front of retroreflective surfaces, and long-wave infrared (LWIR) thermal cameras reveal lingering heat footprints from a hand touch or recently switched-off heaters. Far from being rare edge cases, these are everyday operating conditions that determine whether an embodied agent succeeds or fails.

Yet modern simulators like MuJoCo, Isaac Gym, and CARLA have prioritized rigid-body dynamics and photorealistic graphics while neglecting how the agent actually perceives the world through its sensors. LiDAR is treated as a noiseless distance probe, and thermal imagery is merely pasted on as a static texture. While modality-specific simulators exist (such as ESIM for event cameras), they do not support fair cross-modality comparison.

Driven by the hypothesis that "the physics of perception" (the process from photons to raw measurements) should be modeled with the same fidelity as "the physics of the scene," the authors developed VisionSIM. Covering conventional RGB cameras, SPAD-based direct ToF (dToF), indirect ToF (iToF), event cameras, thermal cameras, and IMUs, VisionSIM provides fine-grained control over physical sensor parameters.

captions.F1: VisionSIM workflow. Ground-truth channels (RGB, depth, normals, optical flow, temperature maps, etc.) are rendered from a single Blender scene and fed into modality-specific physical sensor models to produce realistic raw signals with inherent non-idealities.

sections.heading: Bridging the Gap Between Task-Specific Datasets and General Simulators
sections.summary: Existing datasets and simulation environments are skewed toward specific tasks, simplified rendering, or single-sensor emulation. VisionSIM bridges this gap by offering broad sensor modality coverage alongside physically grounded raw signal fidelity within a single unified pipeline.
sections.details:
Prior research in robot perception and computer vision falls broadly into three categories:

### Task-Specific Datasets and Pipelines
Numerous datasets exist for autonomous driving, optical flow, and stereo matching, but they are built for specific tasks and lack access to raw sensor data, metadata, and comprehensive ground-truth annotations. Moreover, synthetic environments like CARLA struggle to flexibly incorporate emerging modalities such as thermal cameras or single-photon sensors.

### General-Purpose Simulation Engines
Engines like Isaac Gym, Genesis, and Bullet prioritize high-throughput physics for robot reinforcement learning, often sacrificing rendering quality and sensor fidelity. Conversely, tools like BlendProc and Kubric generate photorealistic CG imagery but lack the ability to emulate physical sensor non-idealities.

### Sensor Emulation Techniques
Efforts to emulate specific modalities have advanced, such as v2e for event generation from video, or DIRSIG and MuSES for thermal transport. However, these remain isolated tools, lacking a unified platform for comparing heterogeneous sensor suites in embodied perception. VisionSIM fills this void.

sections.heading: A Two-Layer Architecture Decoupling Rendering from Sensor Emulation
sections.summary: The core architectural innovation of VisionSIM is completely separating the CG rendering "World Simulation Layer" from the "Sensor Emulation Layer." This enables researchers to reuse identical pre-rendered scene data to sweep sensor parameters or test different sensor suites at zero rendering cost.
sections.details:
To maximize computational efficiency and modularity, VisionSIM splits its pipeline into two decoupled layers:

### World Simulation Layer
Built on Blender, this engine renders high-fidelity reference frames alongside comprehensive ground truth: depth, surface normals, optical flow, scene flow, segmentation, lighting components, and camera poses. It also incorporates a GPU-accelerated thermal transport solver that computes transient surface temperature fields simultaneously. Because rendering ultra-high-speed or asynchronous sensors (such as SPADs or event cameras operating at tens of kilohertz) directly would be computationally prohibitive, the layer employs keyframe remapping to dilate animation splines, combined with a "Render-then-Interpolate" strategy that renders at a native scene frame rate and interpolates intermediate frames using deep models like RIFE, dramatically reducing execution time.

### Sensor Emulation Layer
This layer consumes the clean, high-temporal-resolution data and transforms it into realistic sensor measurements based on the physics of each modality. Rather than simply adding ad-hoc Gaussian noise, it formulates the physical phenomena directly—such as photon arrival rates and electron accumulation—allowing modality-specific noise, distortion, and failure modes to emerge naturally as physical consequences. SPAD stochastic binary outputs are stored using bit-packing, achieving 8× lossless compression while allowing random on-the-fly access for downstream deep learning models.

sections.heading: Physically Grounded Sensor Models: Bringing Failure Modes to Light
sections.summary: VisionSIM establishes physically derived forward models for three modalities commonly overlooked by simulators: single-photon LiDAR, indirect ToF, and thermal cameras. It faithfully reproduces photon pileup from dead time, phase wrapping in modulated signals, and emission dynamics driven by thermal diffusivity and history.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Single-Photon (dToF) LiDAR
This system measures photon time-of-flight histograms using a SPAD array. The discrete per-pixel response $T[b]$ sums contributions from scene points within the field of view (FOV) mask $\mathcal{M}$, accounting for albedo $\alpha_p$, inverse-square distance attenuation $1/z_p^2$, and optical efficiency $\eta_{\text{opt}}$. Convolving this with the laser pulse instrument response function (IRF) $g(t)$ and adding the ambient background rate $\lambda_{\text{ambient}}$ yields the photon arrival rate $\lambda(t)$, which is sampled via an inhomogeneous Poisson process. Crucially, the model incorporates detector dead time, where the sensor is temporarily blinded after detecting a photon. Under high flux, early-arriving photons monopolize the detector, causing the histogram to skew forward and underestimating distance—naturally reproducing the real-world "pileup distortion (range walk error)."

### 4.2 Indirect Time-of-Flight (iToF) LiDAR
iToF emits amplitude-modulated light and correlates the reflected signal with multiple phase-shifted demodulation functions to recover distance $\Gamma$ from the phase shift. VisionSIM analytically reproduces "phase wrapping," where objects beyond the unambiguous range $\Gamma_{\text{max}}=c/2f$ (governed by modulation frequency $f$) appear aliased closer; detector "saturation" from electron well limits; contrast loss from ambient light; and "motion artifacts" (boundary tearing and ghosting) caused by scene motion between sequential multi-tap acquisitions.

### 4.3 Thermal (LWIR) Cameras
Long-wave infrared (8–14 $\mu$m) cameras detect thermal emission dictated by Planck's law rather than surface reflectance alone. Surface temperature depends heavily on thermal history rather than instantaneous illumination. VisionSIM calculates absorbed energy from the renderer and solves the heat conduction equation using finite-element methods on the GPU to compute dynamic temperature fields. This captures differing cooling rates across materials with varying thermal diffusivities (ceramic, steel, aluminum) as well as the slow dissipation of thermal handprints.

captions.F2: Indirect ToF (iToF) simulation and failure modes. Top row shows ideal sinusoidal correlation measurements, while the bottom row depicts depth recovery failures caused by modulation frequency mismatch (phase wrapping), sensor saturation, ambient noise, multi-tap motion blur, and quantization noise.

sections.heading: Designing and Analyzing Perception Systems: From Digital Twins to Sensor Selection
sections.summary: The paper showcases three practical case studies: constructing a "digital twin" by identifying parameters from physical LiDAR hardware, "modality migration" to convert existing video datasets into new sensor formats, and "sensor suite benchmarking" for low-light navigation.
sections.details:
### Digital Twin of Real-World Sensors
The authors calibrated VisionSIM parameters against a physical SPAD LiDAR (ADAPS Photonics ADS6311). Because the dToF forward model is differentiable, the instrument response function (IRF) was learned directly via gradient descent using a cross-correlation loss against real histograms. In experiments featuring retroreflective stop signs, intense reflections caused pileup and internal optical stray light caused glare (point cloud ghosting). By accurately modeling these phenomena, the digital twin improved depth estimation RMSE by approximately 1.53 meters, perfectly matching the real sensor's failure behavior.

### Migrating Existing Datasets to New Modalities
By bypassing the World Simulation Layer and feeding third-party video directly into the Sensor Emulation Layer, researchers can synthesize new sensor data without expensive hardware. For instance, feeding CARLA driving video into the SPAD model revealed that a laterally crossing pedestrian induced motion blur in the transient histograms, causing over 3 meters of depth error and resulting in detection failure—uncovering raw-signal-level vulnerabilities.

### Sensor Suite Benchmarking
VisionSIM was used to evaluate candidate sensor suites for a high-speed robot operating in extreme low light before committing to hardware. Two configurations—"standard RGB camera + event camera" versus "passive SPAD camera + IMU"—were emulated along identical high-speed robot arm trajectories for an object detection task (detecting a mug). While the RGB + event suite failed due to severe motion blur and noise, the passive SPAD + IMU suite achieved a 90% confidence detection, demonstrating the power of physically grounded simulation for trade-off analysis under identical conditions.

captions.F4: Three practical applications of VisionSIM: (Top) Building a digital twin by estimating LiDAR IRF and dead time to reproduce pileup and glare; (Middle) Modality migration synthesizing SPAD and event signals from CARLA footage; (Bottom) Benchmark comparison of sensor suites under low-light, high-speed motion.

sections.heading: Sim-to-Real Validation: How Closely Does It Match Physical Hardware?
sections.summary: Sim-to-Real validation was performed across four modalities: thermal, iToF, event, and SPAD cameras. Direct comparisons against real hardware show remarkable agreement, spanning transient heat decay, event firing counts, and photon detection statistics.
sections.details:
To verify fidelity, real-world measurements were compared directly against outputs from VisionSIM digital twins across identical scenes:

- **Thermal Camera (FLIR Boson)**: Tracking the surface temperature of a mug after pouring hot tea over 4 seconds yielded a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of only 7.6% relative to the dynamic temperature range.
- **iToF Camera (Chronoptics)**: Imaging a stop sign resulted in an average phase error of 0.13 radians across the entire $[0, 2\pi]$ range, corresponding to an exceptionally tight depth agreement of ~5.3 cm at 40 MHz modulation.
- **Event Camera (Prophesee EVK4)**: Emulating event rates from auditorium footage yielded discrepancies of only 1.5% for positive events and 5.8% for negative events compared to real hardware.
- **Passive SPAD Camera (Pi-Imaging)**: The simulated average photon detection statistic was 0.221, closely matching the physical measurement of 0.229.

Minor residual discrepancies stem from identifiable boundary condition uncertainties rather than flaws in the sensor models: unmodeled convective heat exchange with ambient air in thermal imaging, hardware multipath and harmonic distortions in iToF, and uncalibrated white balance and radiometric response when emulating from RGB video.

captions.F5: Real-world measurements vs. simulation. Top two rows show thermal and iToF comparisons using full digital twins in Blender; bottom two rows show event and SPAD camera comparisons emulated from co-axially captured standard video.

sections.heading: Release of a Large-Scale, Fully Synchronized Multimodal Indoor Dataset
sections.summary: The authors created and released a multimodal dataset across 100 indoor environments with guaranteed spatial and temporal alignment, providing raw sensor data and dense ground truth for standard cameras, stereo, SPAD, dToF/iToF, thermal cameras, event cameras, and IMUs.
sections.details:
Achieving precise time synchronization and spatial co-registration across heterogeneous sensor rigs in physical experiments is notoriously difficult. Moreover, cutting-edge sensors like high-resolution SPADs are prohibitively expensive and hard to acquire. VisionSIM circumvents these hurdles by generating a comprehensive indoor dataset.

Spanning 100 diverse indoor environments (offices, kitchens, bathrooms, etc.), each scene features a 24-second camera trajectory. The dataset is rendered as HDR stereo pairs at 100 fps and $1000\times 1000$ resolution, comprising 480,000 views complete with fully synchronized ground truth: 6-DoF poses, intrinsics, depth, surface normals, optical flow, scene flow, semantic segmentation, dynamic temperature maps, and direct/indirect illumination buffers.

From these buffers, interpolation yields 16 kHz single-photon streams, 4 kHz event camera streams, 25 fps standard RGB, dToF and iToF LiDAR, thermal imaging, and 250 Hz IMU data. Due to the massive data volume, the complete generation scripts, 3D scene assets, and Docker containers are open-sourced, enabling researchers to regenerate data at custom resolutions or sensor parameters.

sections.heading: Current Limitations and the Road Ahead for Perception Simulation
sections.summary: Decoupling rendering from sensor emulation poses challenges for volumetric scattering (like fog) and wave diffraction (like radar). Currently restricted to open-loop benchmarking, future work aims to integrate with real-time engines for closed-loop robotic control.
sections.details:
While VisionSIM offers substantial capabilities, the authors candidly outline several limitations:

### Architectural Constraints
Decoupling the World Simulation Layer from the Sensor Emulation Layer via intermediate representations (depth, albedo, etc.) provides speed and modularity, but it cannot natively capture complex volumetric effects (such as dense fog or smoke) or high-order optical transport paths. Furthermore, relying on ray-tracing makes it difficult to model wave-optics phenomena like diffraction, posing a challenge for simulating modalities like mmWave radar.

### Scope and Future Directions
All current evaluations are open-loop (generating and evaluating perception data), lacking closed-loop scenarios where robot actions actively feed back into the simulation environment. Additionally, the public dataset is confined to indoor scenes. Future directions include integrating with real-time engines like Unreal Engine to support closed-loop control, expanding to outdoor environments with dynamic weather, and incorporating radio propagation solvers for radar.

sections.heading: Appendix: Distributed Architecture, Transient Thermal Solvers, and Sensor Math
sections.summary: This section details the distributed rendering pipeline, dynamic keyframe remapping, discretization schemes for the GPU thermal transport solver, and the mathematical forward models of each sensor modality.
sections.details:
### Distributed Rendering and Keyframe Remapping
To handle the computational burden of high-frame-rate rendering for ultrafast sensors, VisionSIM uses an RPC-based client/server architecture with UDP broadcast for automatic worker node discovery. To overcome Blender's native frame rate cap, dynamic keyframe remapping scales the time axes of animation curves, enabling physical simulations (such as fluids and rigid bodies) to be sampled at arbitrarily small time steps.

### Formulation of the Thermal Transport Solver
The solver uses absorbed visible power $q_{\text{abs}}(\mathbf{x}, t) = \beta(\mathbf{x}) E(\mathbf{x}, t)$ (where $E$ is diffuse irradiance from the renderer and $\beta$ is surface absorptivity) as the heat source. By linearizing radiative boundary losses, the system matrix for the heat diffusion PDE remains time-invariant across the animation, enabling GPU pre-factorization for ultra-fast solves. To handle hollow or non-manifold mesh assets, interior volumes are populated using Poisson disk sampling with mollified Laplacian operators for point-cloud heat diffusion.

### Bolometer Thermal Inertia and Sensor Dynamics
Microbolometers in thermal cameras possess finite thermal capacitance, resulting in an exponential lag behind incoming radiation. VisionSIM models this by solving a first-order ODE with time constant $\tau$ (typically 5–15 ms), implemented as a single-pole IIR low-pass filter over the rendered radiance stream to faithfully reproduce real-world motion smearing and thermal ghosting.

takeaways: The Sim-to-Real gap in robot perception stems not just from visual graphics, but from simulators ignoring inherent sensor failure modes (pileup, phase wrapping, thermal inertia).
Decoupling scene rendering from sensor physics emulation allows researchers to reuse a single rendering pass to sweep sensor parameters and benchmark suites at zero rendering cost.
Formulating differentiable sensor forward models enables learning physical hardware parameters (e.g., IRF and dead time) directly from real measurements to build accurate digital twins.
Physical sensor models allow rigorous trade-off analysis of heterogeneous sensor configurations in simulation before committing to expensive hardware prototyping.
limitations: Relying on intermediate scene buffers limits the ability to model volumetric scattering (dense fog, smoke) and complex non-line-of-sight light transport.
Ray-tracing foundations cannot easily simulate wave phenomena like diffraction, making integration of modalities like mmWave radar challenging.
Currently evaluated in an open-loop perception regime; closed-loop simulation where robot actions dynamically impact sensor observations is not yet implemented.
The released dataset is restricted to indoor environments, leaving challenging outdoor conditions (harsh weather, variable sunlight) for future work.
